Replacing a conv3x3 with skip loses capacity and hurts on all datasets, unlike replacing 'none'.
Adding skip to an empty edge costs nothing in capacity, so the effect is near zero versus clearly negative when replacing conv.

With edge 2 removed, edge 4 carries more of the node-1 information, so degrading it to pooling hurts more.
Upgrading skip to conv1x1 gives a larger ImageNet16 and CIFAR-100 gain than upgrading 'none' or avg_pool.
With edge 1 intact, edge 5 gets richer inputs from node 2, so upgrading it to conv3x3 gains slightly more than when edge 1 is removed.
Adding conv3x3 on an empty edge 5 restores a path into the output and gives a larger gain than replacing skip.

These hypotheses rest on the 20 experiments plus general knowledge of NAS-Bench-201. Evidence points to three patterns. Edge 3 -> conv3x3 gains most when edge 3 was previously 'none', because it adds a direct connection. Edits that replace a conv with a weaker op (skip, pool) hurt more when the parent has a strong conv at the replaced edge. Edits that add conv capacity matter more when the sibling paths are weak.
